lead: Every thermodynamic quantity you can measure sits inside a partial derivative, and most of those derivatives are not measurable directly. The Jacobian method turns any such derivative into a fixed recipe: write it as a ratio of two Jacobians, expand both in one chosen pair of variables such as (T, P), and read off pressure, volume, temperature and heat-capacity terms. Only a few universities teach it inside this unit, but it removes the guesswork from property relations.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for the four fundamental relations, Chapter 4.3 for Maxwell relations, and the ideal gas law from Unit 2.

sections.h3: The Jacobian and its one key identity

blocks.text: The Jacobian of two functions u(x, y) and v(x, y) is the determinant of the 2×2 matrix of their first partial derivatives.

blocks.where: u and v are any two state functions; x and y are the two independent variables chosen to describe the state; the subscript is the variable held constant.

blocks.text: Swapping the two functions flips the sign, J(u, v) = −J(v, u), and a repeated function gives zero, J(u, u) = 0. Everything else is bookkeeping.

blocks.where: the held-constant variable y appears in both Jacobians. A partial derivative has become a genuine ratio of two determinants.

blocks.text: That identity is the whole method. Partials can now be multiplied and cancelled like fractions, but only in this Jacobian form, never as du/dx.

sections.h3: Cyclic relation and Maxwell relations as ratios

blocks.text: Any target derivative is handled in four steps.

items: Rewrite the target as J(u, y)/J(x, y), with y the variable held constant.
Pick one pair of variables, (T, P) or (T, V), and expand every Jacobian in that same pair.
Cancel the common pair; only P, V, T and heat capacities remain.
Replace any leftover entropy derivative with a Maxwell relation.

blocks.text: The cyclic relation drops out for free. For any three variables x, y, z:

blocks.where: each factor is a ratio of two Jacobians in the same pair, and the three ratios cancel to (−1)³ = −1. The minus sign carries the whole content.

blocks.text: Maxwell relations are Jacobian ratios too. (∂S/∂V)T = J(S, T)/J(V, T); expanding both in (T, P) gives the ratio −(∂S/∂P)T over −(∂V/∂P)T, which the Maxwell relation turns into (∂P/∂T)V. See Chapter 4.3 for the same result from mixed second derivatives.
Take the pressure dependence of enthalpy. From dH = T dS + V dP (Chapter 4.2), at constant T: (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> + V.

The entropy term is a ratio: (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = J(S, T)/J(P, T). Divide numerator and denominator by J(T, V) and expand; the result is −(∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> over −(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>. The Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> leaves (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> divided by (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>, which equals −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.

blocks.where: V is molar volume in m³/mol, T absolute temperature in K, P pressure in Pa; the derivative is taken at constant T.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas V = RT/P and (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = R/P, so the right side is RT/P − RT/P = 0. Enthalpy of an ideal gas is independent of pressure, and its Joule–Thomson coefficient is zero. The same expansion gives the internal pressure, (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P.

spec.title: Jacobian transformation
spec.aria: A target derivative is rewritten as a Jacobian ratio, expanded into pressure–volume–temperature derivatives, and evaluated as a measurable result.

examples.question: Using the Jacobian method, show that (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> for any fluid, then evaluate it for an ideal gas at 300 K with molar volume v = 0.0240 m³/mol. Take R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Write the target as a ratio: (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = J(S, T)/J(V, T).
Expand the numerator in (T, P): J(S, T) = (∂S/∂T)<sub>P</sub>(0) − (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub>(1) = −(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.
Expand the denominator in the same pair: J(V, T) = (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>(0) − (∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>(1) = −(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.
Divide: the two minus signs cancel, leaving (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub>/(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.
Maxwell relation (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, so the ratio is −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>/(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>.
Ideal gas: P = RT/v, so (∂P/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = R/v = 8.314/0.0240 = 346.4 Pa/K.
examples.answer: (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/v = 346.4 Pa/K, that is 346.4 J m⁻³ K⁻¹.
examples.check:
R = 8.314
v = 0.0240
dP_dT = R / v
print(round(dP_dT, 1))

traps: ∂ is not a fraction: (∂u/∂x)<sub>y</sub> cannot be split into du and dx. Only J(u, y)/J(x, y) may be cancelled.
Sign of a swap: J(u, v) = −J(v, u). If you swap the order of the two functions you must also change the sign; swapping the order and forgetting the minus sign gives an answer with the wrong sign.
Mixed variable pairs: both Jacobians must be expanded in the same pair, or nothing cancels.
The cyclic relation equals −1, not +1; writing +1 reverses every derived slope.
Unit slip: v in cm³/mol instead of m³/mol changes R/v by a factor of 10⁶.

quiz.q: Write the determinant definition of J(u, v) in the variables x and y.
State the cyclic relation for three variables x, y, z.
Why is (∂u/∂x)<sub>y</sub> equal to J(u, y)/J(x, y) and not J(u, x)/J(y, x)?
quiz.a: The held-constant variable y must appear in both Jacobians. The second form holds x constant and gives a different derivative.

quiz.q: A gas obeys V = RT/P + b, with b a constant. Find (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.
quiz.a: (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = R/P, so V − T(R/P) = (RT/P + b) − RT/P = b. The derivative equals b at every T and P.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas P = RT/V, evaluate J(P, T) using (T, V) as the pair.
Show that the cyclic relation follows from J(u, v) = −J(v, u).
quiz.a: Each factor is a Jacobian ratio: J(x, z)/J(y, z), J(y, x)/J(z, x), J(z, y)/J(x, y). Each pair differs by one swap, so the product is (−1)³ = −1.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Jacobian technique is the engine behind printed tables of thermodynamic derivatives, and symbolic-algebra software reproduces it in a single line. Research codes that build equations of state use Jacobian ratios to convert measured quantities such as sound speed and thermal expansivity into model parameters. If you go on to process modelling or molecular simulation, search for Bridgman tables, thermodynamic derivative identities, and Jacobian thermodynamic variables.
